To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) Thai tones were discriminated by Thai and Mandarin participants, and that discrimination was better when visual and auditory information was combined than when auditory information only was used; (ii) identification of Thai tones was good in both Thai and Mandarin participants; and (iii) Mandarin participants identified Thai tones in their own tone categories and used visual information to do so.

(a) the auditory and visual information about lexical tone are processed in parallel in the brain, (b) auditory and visual information can be combined to enhance the perception of lexical tone, and (c) the extent of the enhancement depends on the type of tone, the type of task, and the native language of the participants.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the nature of the perceptual processes involved in the discrimination and identification of tone, the role played by visual information in these processes, and the extent to which these processes are influenced by language background and the nature of the tone contrast.
the general features of tones that might contribute towards their categorization and discrimination.
the general properties of tone that contribute to tone categorization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the auditory and visual cues to Thai tones are both important, with visual cues being used especially for tone pairs that are more difficult to discriminate.
lexical tone discrimination and identification in Thai and Mandarin are both influenced by visual information.

the general features of tones that might contribute their categorization are: (i) pitch range (height), (ii) pitch contour (shape), (iii) pitch level, (iv) duration, (v) intensity, (vi) fundamental frequency, and (vii) visual pitch cues.

the auditory-visual integration of lexical tones, as in other domains, is influenced by the nature of the tones and by the native language of the perceiver.

lexical tones can be discriminated and identified by both native and non-native speakers of tone languages, with significant contributions from both auditory and visual modalities.
